claims.text: High-temperature exposure induces selective surface segregation of reactive elements such as Al and Cr in high-entropy alloys.
Segregated reactive elements form a continuous, thermodynamically stable oxide layer.
The continuous oxide layer retards further oxidation.
The initial high-entropy alloy is chemically homogeneous with a near-random distribution of constituent elements.
Exposure at 800–1000°C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere activates the proposed oxidation behavior.
Thermally activated diffusion causes reactive elements to segregate to surfaces or grain boundaries.
Reactive-element-enriched zones provide localized sites for oxide nucleation.
Interdiffusion during high-temperature exposure enriches specific reactive elements at the alloy surface.
The surface-enriched reactive elements oxidize preferentially.
Preferential oxidation of the enriched elements produces a continuous, adherent oxide film.
The continuous, adherent oxide film acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and protects the bulk alloy.
Alloys exhibiting significant reactive-element segregation will develop more uniform and adherent oxide layers with lower oxidation kinetics.
Alloys in which segregation is suppressed will form less protective, discontinuous oxide layers with higher oxidation rates.
Homogenization heat treatments can be used to limit reactive-element segregation.
The mechanism requires a sufficient concentration of reactive elements such as Al or Cr.
The mechanism applies when temperature activates diffusion but does not cause oxide-layer destabilization or a phase transformation that dominates failure.
Comparable oxide uniformity and protective behavior in segregation-minimized and segregation-promoted samples would falsify the proposed causal role of segregation.
